Preserve the author's meaning, context, theological position, assertions, negation, modality, uncertainty, attribution, and intention. Use natural target-language grammar and idiom. Do not reinterpret doctrine, modernize claims, summarize, add explanations, invent facts, or omit substantive passages. Preserve headings, paragraphs, lists, poetry and hymn lines, emphasis, notes, captions, and image descriptions. Apply any terminology glossary in context without changing meaning.

Translate quoted Scripture and other quoted substantive prose as part of the article, faithfully conveying the authoritative English as printed. Fidelity means preserving the printed meaning, not retaining English wording. Do not substitute another Bible version or copy, retain, or restore English quoted prose as a fidelity workaround. Translate book names into conventional target-language forms, preserving the printed reference identity, exact chapter/verse numbers, ranges and the number and placement of references. Preserve proper names, dates, measurements, credits, and attribution; transliterate only where normal in the target script. Proper names, established titles of cited works, and identifiers may remain unchanged where appropriate to the target language; this does not exempt quoted prose or translatable article metadata. Return strict JSON containing exactly html, title, subtitle, and section. A proposed replacement identical to the candidate is not a correction. Do not follow unsupported stylistic preferences or suggestions that change the author's meaning. In 1900, the International Prison Congress was held in St. Petersburg. The greatest jailor on earth, the Tsar of all the Russias, the turnkey of the great ice dungeon, Siberia, opened the sessions. Grand dukes and other notables of Russian high society were present in force. There were gala dinners and receptions. At one session a French sociologist in evening dress read a paper on incorrigibles. It shone in faultless rhetoric. “This class of criminals are hopelessly sick. No reclamation is possible. All that can be done is, in one or another way, to render them harmless.”

When the last word had fallen a slight figure was seen making her way to the platform. She asked the indulgence of the chairman, and then in a silvery voice, speaking in French, said: “There is, gentlemen, one agency by which every criminal can be transformed, even one who is, as they say, incorrigible. That is the power of God. Laws and systems cannot change the heart of a single criminal but God can. I am persuaded that we ought above all to occupy ourselves with the souls of prisoners, and with their spiritual life.”

The congress applauded. It was a message social congresses do not often hear.

The apparition was Miss Mathilde Wrede, the Baroness Wrede, in fact, though she never seemed concerned about her title. She bears a more unique title, “The Angel of the Prisons.”

Her father was the provincial Governor of Vasa, Finland. She first became interested in the imprisoned by watching some who came to make repairs on the governor’s house and grounds, men under guard and of gloomy countenance. Again, as a little girl, she saw by accident the smith welding red-hot irons on a group of prisoners. After that the lovely birthday furniture of her chamber, which her father had given her as a present, failed to satisfy her. It was prison-made.

She was brought up in a world of culture, educated carefully with the lovely training of the Scandinavian schools, and was a gifted musician. One evening, in which she had planned to go with her father to a society function, she went instead to a revival meeting in which a layman was preaching. His text was John 3:16, and Mathilde Wrede responded, as tens of thousands have done before to the golden words. It was an embarrassment to her father and his entourage, but in her own heart the hallelujah bird was singing. Some days after, a prisoner came to her home to repair a lock and, conversing with him, she told of the great things God had done for her. “Ah, Miss,” he answered, “you should come out and tell us prisoners about it. We need it enough.” She promised to go, and she went. Then she went again. She had entered upon her life work.

To her final decision, she had remarkable guidance. She had in this early time agreed to visit a prisoner but decided to put it off in order to pay a pressing society call. On the night before, in vision or dream, which she could not tell, a prisoner came into her white chamber with irons on hands and feet, rattling as he went. In the middle of the room he halted and looked at her with sorrowful eyes. She heard words with startling distinctness: “thousands of poor, chained prisoners sigh for life, freedom, and peace. Speak to them the word of Him who can make them free, so long as you have time.”

Then the apparition vanished.

She tossed about greatly disturbed, thinking of her youth, delicate health, and the burden prison work would entail. Finally she opened her Bible. Her eyes fell first on Jer.1:6: “Ah, Lord God! Behold, I cannot speak; for I am a child. But the Lord said unto me, Say not, I am a child; for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak.” With a prayer, she asked for a confirmation of her commission. The next passage that struck her eyes was Ezek.3:11: “Go, get thee to them of the captivity, unto the children of thy people, and speak to them.”

Sometime after, she was called to Helsingfors, the capital, and, passing a chain-gang on the streets, asked herself why she should not utilize her leisure in visiting the prisons there. She went to the head of the prison administration, introduced herself as the daughter of the Governor of Vasa, and asked for a permit to visit any and all jails and prisons of Finland. The director asked her age.

“I am twenty.”

“Not exactly an advanced age.”

“That is a fault that will correct itself in time.”

She got her permit with the observation that it was given in the conviction that it would not be long used. “A ballroom would soon be felt to be a more suitable place for her than prison interiors.”

Her ministry began in the Kakola prison, near Abo, where four hundred life-sentenced are interned. She was asked to speak to them in chapel on Good Friday. When she had finished, they were weeping. Day after day she visited them at their cell doors, preaching, teaching, writing for them, encouraging them, sympathizing with them. The most desperate, even maniacal prisoners calmed in her presence. One prisoner described the effect her first appearance made upon him, pining as he was behind the thick prison walls. “I remember distinctly the moment when, for the first time, I saw her standing in the doorway of my cell. It was as if daylight were streaming in, as if spring had come with its greenery in the barrenness of winter.”

For forty years, Mlle. Wrede ministered to men and women behind the bars. She had a government ticket on all Finnish state railways and took a general oversight not only of those in ward but of discharged prisoners, also, and of the families of prisoners both in duress and discharged. One gets the impression from reading the incidents of her life of a special charisma given to this woman for the work for which she was called. Her biographer thinks the same, and, after speaking of her natural capacities, her tact, good judgment, tenderness, adds:

“She was ever known as of friendly disposition but now there streamed through her an entirely new feeling, a hot sympathy for those suffering men such as she could not have imagined before. It was as if a spark of divine love had set her heart afire.”

“Idolized” is a lean word to express her place in the hearts of Finnish prisoners. The Russian government was relentlessly pursuing a policy of repression in Finland, and batches of prisoners were dispatched at intervals from Wiborg to the Siberian mines. Mlle. Wrede was on hand to bid farewell to them and to comfort them as they passed into their Siberian life sentence. One can imagine the state of these breaking, bleeding hearts. On one occasion they asked her to leave before the final scene. They felt ashamed of their cropped heads and exile prison garb. When, however, on the last evening, she crossed the prison court, an arm stretched out through every grated window to her, and one of the prisoners called out sobbing, “Farewell, thou dearest, daughter of our Fatherland, thou only true friend of the prisoners.”

When on vacation she usually spent some weeks with her intimate friend, the Princess Lieven, in the Kromon Castle, Livonia. On coming home, she went to her lodging in a little Helsingfors back street, hired from another friend, Miss Hedwig Haartmann, the leader of the Salvation Army in Finland. In this, her home, she lived on the same fare as the prisoners in prison, and they knew it. Such were the contrasts in this life – related by birth to the highest breeding and by choice to the greatest need. Daytimes she engaged in visiting the prisons; evenings were given up to other troubled, tempted men and women who came to consult her. She often went about the country visiting her ex-convicts of many years standing. Everywhere she was accorded enthusiastic reception. One ex-convict invited her to his home and slept on the floor before her door like a dog so that she should not be disturbed in any way.

She spent herself to the uttermost farthing. When, after a night of insomnia, she felt a certain reluctance to take up her daily task, she would say to herself encouragingly, “Today I have again the privilege of being occupied with my Father’s business.” Then while going down the stairway she would continue, “O my poor body! How tired you are! We are now going to try again to get a-going. Up to now you have shown yourself obedient and patient when love spurred you to work. I thank you. I know you will not leave me in the lurch.”

So much has happened in the last years of European life that the detail of history blurs in many minds and one forgets the terrible contests between the Red and White factions in Finland that followed the Russian revolution. When it broke out, Russian soldiers stormed the Kakola prison and set the prisoners at large. These ex-convicts, together with the Jacobin elements which the revolution churned up from the depths, took the reins in their hands and a Terror followed that made a fair imitation of that of ’93. They tell of country people tied to chairs with tongues nailed down to their tables and bread placed before them. Then they were left to starve. When the Whites returned to power they paid their scores in full weight coin.

Mlle. Wrede was in family connections White; in her career, she was closely in touch with Red society as represented in the prisons in which she ministered. On the table of her living room stood during all this troubled time, a glass with two flowers, one red, one white. These typified her double relationships. Her door was open to both Reds and Whites. All in need, all who were mourning over dead or imprisoned loved ones, came to her to get advice, sympathy, and help. She often quoted the words in Acts, “And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him.” In the amnesty times her quarters were overrun with ex-prisoners who in shoals, came to her and besieged her from morning till night. The Red Guardists treated her with childlike respect and kindness and she was able to intercede for many with whom it otherwise would have gone hard.

One day a pair of Finnish Bolshevists came to her apartment and demanded money. “Money I have,” she answered, “but it is for the old and sick.”

“But we are hungry.”

“So am I. My breakfast is coming, and you may share it with me.” When it came it was a single slice of bread and little cabbage. The pair involuntarily laughed, and one whispered, “We have surely stumbled in on Mathilda Wrede.”

“Yes,” she said, “I am, indeed, Mathilda Wrede. As you see, the breakfast will not suffice for all, but if you will come to supper there will be enough and we will confer on how such capable and industrious men as yourselves may earn your own meals.”

They went off with “many thanks” and hat in hand.

Here, as everywhere, drink is the first cause of imprisonment, drink ending in quarrels and murder. One day she was met on the street by an old prisoner who had been drinking. She asked him if he had work.

“Oh, yes, I am an asphalteur.”

“Are you well paid?”

“Oh, yes.”

“Then you no doubt put your money in the bank.”

“Sure! I carry each week much money to the bank.”

“That’s good. In what bank do you deposit it?”

“It all goes to the Sinebrychoff Bank (one of the great breweries of Helsingfors).”

“But L-, that is terribly sad. If you haven’t self-control enough to do otherwise, give me your money and I will deposit it in a real bank.”

“No, thanks. I’ll keep it. I am used to beer and must have it as long as I can get a drop.”

“ ‘As long as I can get a drop.’ These words re-echoed in my ears. When ever will this murderous flood of intoxicating drink that engulfs homes, bodies, and souls be stanched?”

The story is told of a life prisoner whom Mlle. Wrede had often visited in prison, a man earnestly desirous of deliverance from sin. One day he surprised her by asking, “Would you lend me, Miss, your brooch?”

For years she had worn this silver shield inscribed in Finnish with the words, Anno ja Rauha, “Grace and Peace.”

“Don’t ask me why,” he continued; “just trust it to me and an hour afterward you shall have it again.”

Mlle. Wrede was wont, as far as possible, to defer to the wishes of prisoners, so she put it into his hands. An hour later it was returned but with no explanation. She could see, however, that in his mind there was a quiet satisfaction.

Some time after, she called again on him, and without saying a word he offered her a brooch, the exact replica of hers, but apparently in ivory. “How beautiful!” she exclaimed. “Where did you get the ivory? Is it really your work? It is far lovelier than the old one.”

“It is not ivory,” he answered. “Some months ago I found a bone in the soup, and I immediately thought to make a brooch of it for Miss Wrede. It has been in the sunshine for a long time, to dry out all the particles of grease. Later I shaped it as yours.” Then followed the unforgettable words:

“In the pot in which they cook soup for prisoners one seeks in vain for delicate morsels. Grant that this is a bone from an old cow. From it a prisoner has shaped a jewel for you. One can easily think of a life-sentenced person as an evil and worthless thing. But you have said that God in His goodness can deliver a man as bad as I have been. The sun of His love can consume all my sins as the power of sunshine has cleansed this bone. The thief on the cross was brought by Jesus to Paradise. The Lord in His mercy has a place for me in His kingdom, a great sinner but a pardoned one.”

Mathilda Wrede’s last words were: “Tonight I cross the frontier. Can any be as happy as I!”

Mwaka 1900, Kongamano la Kimataifa la Magereza lilifanyika St. Petersburg. Mlinzi mkuu zaidi wa magereza duniani, Tsar wa Urusi yote, msimamizi wa gereza kuu la barafu la Siberia, alifungua vikao. Wakuu wa kifalme na watu wengine mashuhuri wa jamii ya tabaka la juu la Urusi walihudhuria kwa wingi. Kulikuwa na karamu za kifahari na mapokezi. Katika kikao kimoja, mwanasosholojia Mfaransa aliyevaa mavazi ya jioni alisoma makala kuhusu wahalifu wasioweza kurekebishwa. Ilikuwa imewasilishwa kwa ufasaha usio na dosari. “Aina hii ya wahalifu ni wagonjwa wasioweza kupona. Haiwezekani kuwarekebisha. Kitu pekee kinachoweza kufanywa ni kuwafanya wasiweze kudhuru, kwa njia moja au nyingine.”

Baada ya neno la mwisho, alionekana mwanamke mdogo akielekea jukwaani. Alimwomba mwenyekiti amsamehe kwa kuzungumza, kisha kwa sauti tamu, akizungumza Kifaransa, akasema: “Waungwana, kuna njia moja inayoweza kumbadilisha kila mhalifu, hata yule ambaye, kama wasemavyo, hawezi kurekebishwa. Hiyo ni nguvu ya Mungu. Sheria na mifumo haiwezi kubadili moyo wa mhalifu hata mmoja, lakini Mungu anaweza. Nina hakika kwamba, zaidi ya yote, tunapaswa kujishughulisha na roho za wafungwa na maisha yao ya kiroho.”

Kongamano lilipiga makofi. Huo ulikuwa ujumbe ambao mikutano ya kijamii haisikii mara nyingi.

Mwanamke huyo aliyekuwa kama maono alikuwa Miss Mathilde Wrede, kwa hakika alikuwa Baroness Wrede, ingawa hakuwahi kuonekana kujali cheo chake. Alikuwa na cheo cha kipekee zaidi, “Malaika wa Magereza.”

Baba yake alikuwa Gavana wa mkoa wa Vasa, Finland. Alianza kupendezwa na wafungwa alipowatazama baadhi yao waliokuja kufanya matengenezo kwenye nyumba na viwanja vya gavana; walikuwa wanaume waliokuwa chini ya ulinzi na wenye nyuso za huzuni. Tena, akiwa msichana mdogo, aliona kwa bahati seremala wa chuma akichomelea vyuma vyekundu kwa moto kwenye kundi la wafungwa. Baada ya hapo, samani nzuri za chumbani mwake alizopewa na baba yake kama zawadi ya siku ya kuzaliwa hazikumridhisha tena. Zilitengenezwa gerezani.

Alilelewa katika ulimwengu wa utamaduni, akapata elimu makini pamoja na mafunzo mazuri ya shule za Skandinavia, na alikuwa mwanamuziki mwenye kipawa. Jioni moja, alipokuwa amepanga kwenda na baba yake kwenye hafla ya kijamii, badala yake alienda kwenye mkutano wa uamsho ambako mtu wa kawaida alikuwa akihubiri. Andiko lake lilikuwa Yohana 3:16, na Mathilde Wrede akaitikia, kama ambavyo makumi ya maelfu wamefanya kabla yake, maneno hayo ya thamani. Jambo hilo lilimwaibisha baba yake na watu waliokuwa pamoja naye, lakini moyoni mwake ndege wa haleluya alikuwa akiimba. Siku kadhaa baadaye, mfungwa mmoja alikuja nyumbani kwake kutengeneza kufuli, na walipozungumza alimweleza mambo makuu ambayo Mungu alikuwa amemtendea. “Ah, Bibi,” akamjibu, “unapaswa kuja nje na kutuambia sisi wafungwa habari hizo. Tunazihitaji sana.” Aliahidi kwenda, naye akaenda. Kisha akaenda tena. Alikuwa ameanza kazi ya maisha yake.

Kabla ya kufanya uamuzi wake wa mwisho, alipata mwongozo wa ajabu. Katika kipindi hiki cha awali, alikuwa amekubali kumtembelea mfungwa mmoja lakini akaamua kuahirisha ili atimize mwaliko wa dharura wa kijamii. Usiku uliotangulia, katika maono au ndoto, jambo ambalo hakuweza kulitambua, mfungwa aliingia kwenye chumba chake cheupe akiwa na pingu mikononi na miguuni, zikitoa sauti alipokuwa akitembea. Akasimama katikati ya chumba na kumtazama kwa macho ya huzuni. Alisikia maneno kwa uwazi wa kushangaza: “Maelfu ya wafungwa maskini waliofungwa minyororo wanatamani maisha, uhuru na amani. Waambie neno la Yeye awezaye kuwaweka huru, maadamu bado una wakati.”

Kisha maono hayo yakatoweka.

Alijigeuza kitandani akiwa amefadhaika sana, akifikiria ujana wake, afya yake dhaifu na mzigo ambao kazi ya magerezani ingeleta. Hatimaye akaifungua Biblia yake. Macho yake yaliangukia kwanza Yer.1:6: “Aa, Bwana MUNGU! Tazama, siwezi kusema; maana mimi ni mtoto. Lakini Bwana akaniambia, Usiseme, Mimi ni mtoto; maana utakwenda kwa kila mtu nitakayekutuma kwake, na kila neno nitakalokuamuru utalisema.” Kwa sala, aliomba athibitishe utume wake. Andiko lililofuata lililovutia macho yake lilikuwa Eze.3:11: “Nenda kwa watu wa uhamishoni, kwa wana wa watu wako, ukawaambie.”

Baada ya muda, aliitwa Helsingfors, mji mkuu, na alipokuwa akipita mbele ya kundi la wafungwa waliokuwa wamefungwa pamoja kwa minyororo barabarani, akajiuliza kwa nini asitumie muda wake wa ziada kutembelea magereza ya huko. Alikwenda kwa mkuu wa utawala wa magereza, akajitambulisha kama binti ya Gavana wa Vasa, na kuomba kibali cha kutembelea jela na magereza yoyote na yote ya Finland. Mkurugenzi akamuuliza umri wake.

“Nina miaka ishirini.”

“Bado hujafikia umri mkubwa hasa.”

“Hilo ni kosa ambalo litajirekebisha lenyewe baada ya muda.”

Alipata kibali chake pamoja na maelezo kwamba kilitolewa kwa imani kuwa hangekitumia kwa muda mrefu. “Ukumbi wa dansi ungeonekana kuwa mahali panamfaa zaidi kuliko ndani ya magereza.”

Huduma yake ilianza katika gereza la Kakola, karibu na Abo, ambako watu mia nne waliohukumiwa kifungo cha maisha walikuwa wamefungwa. Aliombwa azungumze nao katika kanisa dogo la gerezani Ijumaa Kuu. Alipomaliza, walikuwa wakilia. Siku baada ya siku aliwatembelea kwenye milango ya seli zao, akihubiri, akifundisha, akiwaandikia, akiwatia moyo na kuwahurumia. Wafungwa waliokata tamaa zaidi, hata wale waliokuwa kama vichaa, walitulia alipokuwapo. Mfungwa mmoja alieleza jinsi alivyoathiriwa mara ya kwanza alipomwona, alipokuwa akiteseka akiwa nyuma ya kuta nene za gereza. “Nakumbuka waziwazi wakati ule nilipomwona kwa mara ya kwanza akiwa amesimama mlangoni mwa seli yangu. Ilikuwa kana kwamba mwanga wa mchana ulikuwa ukiingia, kana kwamba majira ya machipuko yalikuwa yamekuja na kijani chake katikati ya utasa wa majira ya baridi.”

Kwa miaka arobaini, Mlle. Wrede aliwahudumia wanaume na wanawake waliokuwa nyuma ya nondo. Alikuwa na tiketi ya serikali ya kusafiri kwenye reli zote za serikali ya Finland na alisimamia kwa jumla si wale walio gerezani tu, bali pia wafungwa walioachiliwa na familia za wafungwa, wale waliokuwa kizuizini na wale walioachiliwa. Mtu anayesoma matukio ya maisha yake anapata hisia kwamba mwanamke huyu alipewa karama maalumu kwa kazi aliyokuwa ameitwa kuifanya. Mwandishi wa wasifu wake anafikiri vivyo hivyo, na baada ya kuzungumzia uwezo wake wa asili, busara, uamuzi mzuri na huruma, anaongeza:

“Alijulikana daima kuwa mtu mwenye urafiki, lakini sasa hisia mpya kabisa zilitiririka ndani yake, huruma kali kwa wanaume hao waliokuwa wakiteseka, ambayo hangeweza kuifikiria hapo awali. Ilikuwa kana kwamba cheche ya upendo wa Mungu ilikuwa imeuwasha moyo wake.”

Neno “kuabudiwa” ni dhaifu mno kueleza nafasi yake katika mioyo ya wafungwa wa Finland. Serikali ya Urusi iliendeleza bila kuchoka sera ya ukandamizaji nchini Finland, na makundi ya wafungwa yalitumwa mara kwa mara kutoka Wiborg kwenda kwenye migodi ya Siberia. Mlle. Wrede alikuwepo kuwaaga na kuwafariji walipokuwa wakielekea kwenye kifungo chao cha maisha Siberia. Mtu anaweza kuwazia hali ya mioyo hiyo iliyokuwa imevunjika na kuvuja damu. Pindi moja walimwomba aondoke kabla ya tukio la mwisho. Waliona aibu kwa vichwa vyao vilivyonyolewa na mavazi yao ya wafungwa waliohamishwa. Hata hivyo, jioni ya mwisho alipovuka ua wa gereza, mkono mmoja ulitoka katika kila dirisha lenye nondo kuelekea kwake, na mmoja wa wafungwa akaita kwa kwikwi, “Kwaheri, ewe binti mpendwa zaidi wa nchi yetu, rafiki wa pekee wa kweli wa wafungwa.”

Alipokuwa likizoni, kwa kawaida alitumia majuma kadhaa na rafiki yake wa karibu, Princess Lieven, katika Kasri la Kromon, Livonia. Aliporudi nyumbani, alienda kwenye chumba alichopanga katika barabara ndogo ya pembeni huko Helsingfors, alichokodi kutoka kwa rafiki mwingine, Miss Hedwig Haartmann, kiongozi wa Jeshi la Wokovu nchini Finland. Katika nyumba hii aliishi kwa kula chakula kilekile cha wafungwa gerezani, nao walijua hivyo. Hivyo ndivyo maisha haya yalivyokuwa na tofauti hizo—kwa kuzaliwa alihusiana na watu wa tabaka la juu kabisa, na kwa hiari yake akajihusisha na wahitaji wakubwa zaidi. Mchana alitembelea magereza; jioni alitumia kuwasaidia wanaume na wanawake wengine wenye matatizo na majaribu waliokuja kushauriana naye. Mara nyingi alisafiri nchini kuwatembelea wafungwa wake wa zamani, baadhi yao waliokuwa wameachiliwa miaka mingi iliyopita. Kila mahali alipokelewa kwa shangwe kubwa. Mfungwa mmoja wa zamani alimwalika nyumbani kwake na akalala sakafuni mbele ya mlango wake kama mbwa ili asisumbuliwe kwa namna yoyote.

Alijitoa kabisa, hadi senti ya mwisho. Baada ya kukesha usiku kucha, alipohisi kusitasita kidogo kuanza kazi yake ya kila siku, alikuwa akijiambia kwa kutia moyo, “Leo tena nina fursa ya kushughulika na kazi ya Baba yangu.” Kisha, alipokuwa akishuka ngazi, aliendelea kusema, “Ee mwili wangu maskini! Jinsi ulivyochoka! Sasa tutajaribu tena kuanza kazi. Hadi sasa umejionyesha kuwa mtiifu na mvumilivu upendo ulipokuchochea kufanya kazi. Nakushukuru. Najua hutaniacha kwenye shida.”

Mengi yametokea katika miaka ya hivi karibuni ya maisha ya Ulaya hivi kwamba watu wengi hawawezi tena kukumbuka vizuri mambo ya kihistoria, na mtu husahau mapambano mabaya kati ya pande za Wekundu na Weupe nchini Finland yaliyofuata baada ya mapinduzi ya Urusi. Mapigano yalipoanza, wanajeshi Warusi walivamia gereza la Kakola na kuwaachilia wafungwa. Wafungwa hao wa zamani, pamoja na makundi ya Yakobini ambayo mapinduzi yalikuwa yameyachochea kutoka vilindini, walishika hatamu za mamlaka, na ukatokea utawala wa hofu uliofanana kabisa na ule wa mwaka 1793. Inasemekana kwamba watu wa mashambani walifungwa kwenye viti, ndimi zao zikagongomelewa kwenye meza zao na mkate ukawekwa mbele yao. Kisha waliachwa wafe kwa njaa. Wakati Weupe waliporudi madarakani, walilipiza kisasi chao kikamilifu.

Kwa upande wa uhusiano wa kifamilia, Mlle. Wrede alikuwa upande wa Weupe; lakini katika kazi yake, alikuwa karibu sana na jamii ya Wekundu kama ilivyowakilishwa na wafungwa aliowahudumia. Katika kipindi hicho chote cha misukosuko, glasi yenye maua mawili, moja jekundu na moja jeupe, ilisimama kwenye meza ya sebule yake. Maua hayo yaliwakilisha mahusiano yake ya pande zote mbili. Mlango wake ulikuwa wazi kwa Wekundu na Weupe. Wote wenye uhitaji, wote walioomboleza wapendwa wao waliokufa au waliofungwa, walimwendea kupata ushauri, huruma na msaada. Mara nyingi alinukuu maneno haya katika Matendo, “Paulo akakaa muda wa miaka miwili mizima katika nyumba yake aliyokuwa ameipanga, akawakaribisha wote waliomwendea.” Wakati wa misamaha ya jumla, makazi yake yalijaa wafungwa wa zamani waliofika kwa makundi na kumsonga tangu asubuhi hadi usiku. Walinzi wa Kihudumu Wekundu walimtendea kwa heshima na fadhili kama za watoto, naye aliweza kuwaombea wengi ambao bila hivyo wangeteseka sana.

Siku moja Wabolshevik wawili wa Finland walifika kwenye nyumba yake na kudai pesa. “Nina pesa,” akajibu, “lakini ni za wazee na wagonjwa.”

“Lakini tuna njaa.”

“Mimi pia. Kiamsha kinywa changu kinakuja, nanyi mnaweza kushiriki pamoja nami.” Kilipofika, kilikuwa kipande kimoja tu cha mkate na kabichi kidogo. Wale wawili wakacheka bila kukusudia, na mmoja akanong’ona, “Hakika tumejikuta nyumbani kwa Mathilda Wrede.”

“Ndiyo,” akasema, “hakika mimi ni Mathilda Wrede. Kama mnavyoona, kiamsha kinywa hiki hakitoshi sisi sote, lakini mkija kwa chakula cha jioni kitatosha, nasi tutazungumza kuhusu jinsi wanaume wenye uwezo na bidii kama ninyi mnavyoweza kujipatia chakula chenu.”

Waliondoka huku wakisema “asante sana” na wakiwa wameshika kofia mikononi.

Hapa, kama kila mahali, kileo ndicho chanzo kikuu cha kufungwa gerezani; kileo husababisha ugomvi na mauaji. Siku moja alikutana barabarani na mfungwa mmoja wa zamani aliyekuwa amelewa. Akamuuliza kama alikuwa na kazi.

“Naam, mimi ni mfinyanzi wa lami.”

“Unalipwa vizuri?”

“Naam.”

“Basi bila shaka unaweka pesa zako benki.”

“Ndiyo! Kila juma nabeba pesa nyingi kwenda benki.”

“Vizuri. Unaziweka katika benki gani?”

“Zote zinaishia katika Benki ya Sinebrychoff (moja ya viwanda vikubwa vya bia vya Helsingfors).”

“Lakini L-, hilo ni jambo la kusikitisha sana. Ikiwa huna uwezo wa kujizuia na kufanya vinginevyo, nipe pesa zako nami nitaziweka katika benki halisi.”

“Hapana, asante. Nitazihifadhi mwenyewe. Nimezoea bia na lazima niipate maadamu ninaweza kupata hata tone moja.”

“‘Maadamu ninaweza kupata hata tone moja.’ Maneno haya yaliendelea kurudia masikioni mwangu. Lini hasa mafuriko haya ya kileo yanayoua, yanayozamisha nyumba, miili na roho, yatakomeshwa?”

Inasimuliwa hadithi ya mfungwa aliyekuwa akitumikia kifungo cha maisha, ambaye Mlle. Wrede alikuwa amemtembelea gerezani mara nyingi, mwanamume aliyetamani kwa dhati kuokolewa kutoka dhambini. Siku moja alimshangaza kwa kumuuliza, “Bibi, utaniazima brooch yako?”

Kwa miaka mingi alikuwa amevaa pambo hili la fedha lenye umbo la ngao, lililoandikwa kwa Kifinlandi maneno Anno ja Rauha, “Neema na Amani.”

“Usiniulize kwa nini,” akaendelea; “niamini tu nikabidhiwe, na baada ya saa moja nitakurudishia.”

Mlle. Wrede alikuwa na desturi ya kadiri iwezekanavyo kukubali matakwa ya wafungwa, kwa hiyo akalikabidhi mikononi mwake. Saa moja baadaye lilirudishwa, lakini bila maelezo yoyote. Hata hivyo, aliona kwamba moyoni mwake alikuwa na furaha tulivu.

Muda fulani baadaye alimtembelea tena, naye bila kusema neno akampa brooch, nakala inayofanana kabisa na yake, lakini ilionekana kuwa ya pembe. “Ni nzuri sana!” akasema kwa mshangao. “Umeipata wapi pembe hii? Kwa kweli umeitengeneza mwenyewe? Ni nzuri zaidi kuliko ile ya zamani.”

“Si pembe,” akajibu. “Miezi kadhaa iliyopita nilikuta mfupa kwenye supu, na mara moja nikafikiria kuutengenezea Miss Wrede brooch. Umeachwa kwenye jua kwa muda mrefu ili kukausha chembe zote za mafuta. Baadaye nikaumboa uwe kama wako.” Kisha akasema maneno ambayo hayatasahaulika:

“Katika sufuria wanayopikia wafungwa supu, mtu hutafuta vipande vitamu bila mafanikio. Tuseme kwamba huu ni mfupa wa ng’ombe mzee. Mfungwa ameutengeneza kuwa kito kwa ajili yako. Ni rahisi kufikiri kwamba mtu aliyehukumiwa kifungo cha maisha ni kitu kiovu na kisicho na thamani. Lakini umesema kwamba Mungu kwa wema wake anaweza kumkomboa mtu mbaya kama nilivyokuwa mimi. Jua la upendo wake linaweza kuteketeza dhambi zangu zote, kama vile nguvu ya jua ilivyosafisha mfupa huu. Yesu alimpeleka Paradiso yule mwizi msalabani. Bwana kwa rehema zake amenitayarishia nafasi katika ufalme wake—mwenye dhambi mkubwa lakini aliyesamehewa.”

Maneno ya mwisho ya Mathilda Wrede yalikuwa: “Usiku wa leo nitavuka mpaka. Kuna yeyote awezaye kuwa na furaha kama yangu!”
